title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Learn Meaningful Concept Hierarchies?
claim: Flat, unordered concept spaces lack relations and force piecemeal steering; explicit hierarchies enable interpretable, consistent, automated steering.
layout: 2 panels split by vertical line, left-to-right; flat list vs tree
description: Two side-by-side panels separated by a vertical black line. Left, titled 'Unordered Concept Space': an input vector (gray stacked squares) feeds a blue trapezoid labeled M, which outputs a flat vertical list of circles, each paired with a small photo and label (Tennis, Pine Cone, Tomato, Racket, Pine, Tennis Serve). Two circles are filled yellow with pencil icons for individual steering. A dashed gray curved arrow marks missing relations. Right, titled 'Hierarchical Concept Representation': the same input feeds a trapezoid M_H, which outputs tree graphs (Plants→Pine→Pine Cone, Tomato; Sport→Tennis, Baseball; Tennis→Racket, Court, Serve) with photos. Black arrows show explicit relations. Yellow nodes and gold arrows show one edit on Serve propagating up to Tennis and Sport. Legends sit at the bottom of each panel.
caption: Hierarchical concept representations explicitly model relations between concepts and allow for consistent model steering. Typical unsupervised concept discovery approaches (left) provide large and unordered concept spaces. These lack clear connections between concepts, making interpretation difficult and cumbersome. Similarly, model steering requires identifying and updating many concepts at once. Hierarchical concept representations (right) instead explicitly provide a hierarchy graph for interpretation as well as consistent and automated model steering.
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for unsupervised concept discovery in large models. To make the resulting feature spaces more interpretable and manageable, recent approaches have begun imposing hierarchical structure, either explicitly or as an implicit effect of training constraints, yet rigorous comparison remains difficult. There are no agreed-upon requirements for what a meaningful feature hierarchy should satisfy, and evaluation has largely relied on qualitative illustrations with fragmented quantitative protocols. To address this, we derive a set of key requirements for generalization/specialization hierarchies in unsupervised concept discovery, drawing on semantic net and taxonomy research alongside recent SAE work, and use them to derive a concrete evaluation protocol. Applying this protocol to current SAE approaches trained on visual data, we find that while feature spaces generally provide a basis for sensible hierarchies, establishing good hierarchical structure remains challenging. In particular, feature absorption, both in its well-known hard form and in a continuous, soft form, systematically compromises hierarchy quality, pointing to a fundamental tension that future approaches will need to navigate.
